intro: Sung every night of Chanukah once the candles are lit, and the tune is one of the few in the Ashkenazi repertoire that everyone in the room already knows. What is less known is the shape of the poem: six stanzas, each about a different exile — Egypt, Babylon, Haman, the Greeks — and the acrostic of the first letters spells the poet's name. Most tables sing the first stanza and stop, which is a pity, because the first stanza is the only one that is not about history.

stanzas.label: the dedication

lines.en: Rock of my salvation, it is fitting to praise You.
Let my house of prayer be established, and there we will offer thanks.
When You prepare the slaughter of the blaspheming foe,
then I will finish, with a song of psalm, the dedication of the altar.

stanzas.summary: Four lines that rhyme on the same syllable — {{0.5}}, {{1.5}}, {{2.4}}, {{3.5}} all end in -be-ach — and that rhyme is doing an argument. {{3.4}} is the word chanukah itself: dedication. The poem announces its own subject in its last word, and the festival is named after it.

stanzas.label: Egypt

lines.en: My soul was sated with troubles, my strength consumed with grief.
They embittered my life with hardship, under the rule of the calf-kingdom.
But with His great hand He brought out the treasured people,
the army of Pharaoh and all his seed went down like a stone into the deep.

stanzas.summary: {{7.5}} and {{7.6}} are lifted straight out of the Song of the Sea in Exodus 15, where the same two words close the same image. The poem quotes rather than describes, and it will do this in every stanza.

stanzas.label: Babylon

lines.en: He brought me to His holy sanctuary, and even there I found no rest.
An oppressor came and exiled me, for I had served strangers,
and I drank wine of poison; I had barely passed through
when Babylon's end came through Zerubbabel; after seventy years I was saved.

stanzas.summary: {{11.1}} and {{11.2}} sit side by side on purpose: the name of the empire and the name of the man who ended it share three consonants. The poem is built out of that kind of pun, and it is a great deal easier to remember a stanza when you can hear the joke in it.

stanzas.label: Haman

lines.en: The Agagite, son of Hammedatha, sought to cut down the tall cypress,
but it became a snare and a trap for him, and his arrogance was stilled.
You lifted the head of the Benjaminite, and blotted out the enemy's name;
the many sons he had, and his possessions, You hanged on the gallows.

stanzas.summary: {{12.2}} is a cypress, and it means Mordechai — the poem never names him, it calls him a tall tree, and then {{14.1}} names his tribe instead. Naming by association rather than directly is the ordinary manner of a piyyut, and it is why these poems reward a second reading.

stanzas.label: the Greeks

lines.en: The Greeks gathered against me, then, in the days of the Hasmoneans,
and they breached the walls of my towers, and defiled all the oils.
And from the one jar that remained, a miracle was done for the roses.
Men of understanding fixed eight days for song and rejoicing.

stanzas.summary: This is the only stanza about Chanukah, and it arrives fifth. {{18.4}} — roses — is the poem's word for the people of Israel, and {{19.3}} is the number eight, which is the whole festival in one word. Everything a household actually celebrates this week is compressed into four lines out of twenty-four.

stanzas.label: the plea

lines.en: Bare Your holy arm and bring near the end of the salvation.
Avenge the blood of Your servants upon the wicked nation,
for the hour has grown long for us, and there is no end to the days of evil.
Thrust back the red one into the deepest shadow; raise up for us the seven shepherds.

stanzas.summary: The sixth stanza is often omitted from printed siddurim and from most tables, and it is the one place the poem stops narrating and starts demanding. Whether to sing it is a decision each household makes; it is printed here because a poem with its last stanza removed is a different poem.

chantTips: Everyone sings the first stanza. Whether the table goes on to the other five is a household habit — ask before you launch into the second.
The melody is strophic: the same eight bars carry all six stanzas, so once you have the first you have all of them.
Lines one and two are the question, lines three and four are the answer. Let the voice lift at the end of line two and settle at the end of line four.
It is sung standing, in front of the candles, immediately after the blessings and while the flames are still small.
Around 96 BPM in a room; slower if the group is mostly reading it off a page for the first time.

about.body: The first letters of the five original stanzas spell the name Mordechai. The sixth stanza does not fit that acrostic and is generally taken to be a later addition, which is one reason it is printed in some editions and not others.

Egypt, Babylon, Haman, the Greeks, and then the present. Chanukah occupies one stanza of five. The poem treats the festival as one entry in a series rather than as its subject, and the last stanza makes the series open-ended.

The melody now sung almost everywhere in the Ashkenazi world is a much later borrowing than the words, which are medieval. It is not reproduced here, and it does not need to be: you will hear it the first night you are in anyone's home during the festival.

The Hebrew on this page is the Daat Siddur Ashkenaz text, in the public domain, taken from Sefaria and pinned in this repository. Two variant readings marked in that edition were removed rather than printed, since they are alternatives to a word and not extra words to sing.
